semantic_correction.stem: After several prolonged work periods, an RN notices marked fatigue and difficulty maintaining attention during the current shift and is concerned that alertness may no longer support safe care. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Report the fatigue-related safety concern promptly and work with the charge nurse or supervisor to obtain appropriate workload or assignment mitigation.
options.B: Continue the assignment without reporting the fatigue as long as no medication error or client injury has occurred during the current shift.
options.C: Use caffeine and brief personal breaks as the complete response, because fatigue from prolonged work hours is primarily an individual wellness issue.
options.D: Transfer the remaining assessments and clinical decisions to available assistive personnel so the RN can reduce workload without changing the assignment.

semantic_correction.rationale: The American Nurses Association position statement effective May 27, 2026 describes nurse fatigue as a nurse- and patient-safety crisis and a shared individual, employer, and organizational responsibility. ANA specifically states that nurses and employers should monitor physical and mental capacity needed for safe care, that organizations must implement fatigue-mitigation strategies, and that employers should create conditions in which nurses can monitor and report fatigue without fear of punitive consequences. ANA staffing principles also state that RNs have a professional obligation to report unsafe conditions or inappropriate staffing that adversely affect safe, quality care. The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan requires the RN to recognize limitations and use resources, organize workload, and provide safe client care. A therefore best addresses an identified safety impairment by promptly reporting the concern and seeking appropriate workload/assignment mitigation through the supervisory process. B waits for harm before acting. C treats a shared safety problem as exclusively personal and may not restore safe alertness. D improperly transfers nursing assessments and clinical decisions to assistive personnel. Therefore A is correct.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: When fatigue may impair safe nursing performance, promptly communicate the safety concern and use organizational/supervisory resources to obtain appropriate workload or assignment mitigation rather than concealing fatigue, waiting for harm, or delegating nursing judgment.
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Addressing Nurse Fatigue to Promote Health, Safety, and Well-Being for All; Principles for Nurse Staffing
semantic_correction.source_version_date: ANA fatigue position statement effective May 27, 2026; current ANA staffing guidance accessed 2026-08-19
semantic_correction.source_locator: Fatigue position statement — fatigue is a patient/nurse safety crisis; shared nurse/employer responsibility; monitor physical and mental capacity; employers enable fatigue reporting without fear and implement mitigation. Staffing principles — RNs should report unsafe conditions/inappropriate staffing affecting safe quality care; shift/overtime policies should prevent fatigue-related errors
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Fatigue that threatens alertness is a patient-safety concern requiring prompt recognition/reporting and shared organizational mitigation rather than being treated solely as a private wellness issue.
semantic_correction.blueprint_locator: Management of Care — recognize limitations of self and others and utilize resources; organize workload to manage time effectively; provide/direct nursing care that enhances the care-delivery setting and protects clients and health care personnel
semantic_correction.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — fatigue-related safety escalation and resource use
semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: replaced passive recall of ANA fatigue guidance with a direct staff-RN patient-safety action. Removed the absolute-word and answer-length cues and required prompt fatigue reporting plus appropriate workload/assignment mitigation without delegating nursing judgment.

audit_findings_append.finding: The final item tests what the RN does when fatigue threatens safe alertness, directly linking self-limitation recognition to supervisory resource use.

scope_exclusions.automatic_assignment_refusal: Not asserted; the RN reports the safety concern and seeks appropriate mitigation through the organizational process.
scope_exclusions.fatigue_as_personal_failure: Not asserted; ANA explicitly frames fatigue as a shared systems and individual safety responsibility.
scope_exclusions.delegation_of_nursing_judgment: Not permitted by the correct response.

near_duplicate_check.note: Q0520 tests escalation of missed-care risk after acute client deterioration; Q0427 tests ICU assignment/workload reassessment; Q0272 tests unit-level work-system drivers of worker well-being. Q0577 tests the RN's immediate action when personal fatigue itself may compromise safe alertness.

option_audit.A: Correct; reports an active safety concern and uses supervisory/organizational mitigation.
option_audit.B: Plausible persistence response but waits for an actual error or injury rather than acting on identified impairment risk.
option_audit.C: Plausible self-management response but incorrectly treats organizationally driven fatigue as fully solved by personal measures.
option_audit.D: Plausible workload-reduction response but transfers nursing judgment outside assistive-personnel role.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. The stem states that fatigue may no longer support safe care. A alone communicates the active risk and uses appropriate resources; B delays until harm, C treats mitigation as purely personal, and D delegates nursing judgment.

cueing_check.note: Correct A is one character shorter than D and three characters longer than C; no conspicuous length cue remains.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: Recognizing self-limitations, using resources, workload management and safe-care responsibility are explicit Management of Care activities.

checks: fatigue reporting without punitive consequence principle verified
ANA staffing unsafe-condition reporting principle verified
